def: A machine that can sense, think and act, all on its own.
Notice the world with sensors, like a camera or a touch sensor. The first of a robot's three jobs.
Decide what to do. A robot's computer and its rules do the thinking.
Do something: drive wheels, move an arm, fire thrusters. Motors do most of the acting.
A robot's senses: parts that notice the world, like cameras, touch sensors and ultrasonic sensors.
A sensor that sees colors and shapes, like your eyes. It can't see in the dark.
A sensor that feels when the robot bumps into something.
A sensor that feels tilting and turning, like your inner ear.
A sensor that measures distance with sound: it chirps, then times how long the echo takes to come back.
Sound that bounces back off something. An ultrasonic sensor times the echo to work out the distance.
How an ultrasonic sensor's chirp spreads out, like a flashlight beam. It reports the closest thing anywhere inside the cone.
A sensor that measures distance with flashes of laser light. Many lidars spin to measure the whole room.
The map a spinning lidar makes: thousands of measured dots put together.
A sensor that shines invisible light, like a TV remote, and measures what bounces back. It only works up close, and black things and clear glass fool it.
Using more than one kind of sensor, so when one gets fooled, another catches it.
An instruction a robot follows: IF something is true, THEN do something. It checks its rules from the top, and the first true one wins.
A motor that spins whenever electricity flows through it. Fast, but weak without a gearbox.
Turns per minute: how fast something spins.
Twisting strength: how hard something turns or twists. For an arm, torque = weight × sideways distance.
Gears that trade a motor's speed for strength (torque): the wheel turns slower but pushes harder.
How many times the motor turns for each turn of the wheel. With 20:1, the wheel turns 20 times slower and pushes about 20 times harder.
More gearing (a bigger ratio, like 12:1) is slower but pushes harder. Less gearing (like 4:1) is faster but weaker.
When the load is too heavy, the motor stops turning even though the power is on.
A motor that moves to an angle you choose, then holds it there. A position sensor inside checks the angle.
The part inside a servo that measures which way it's pointing.
Pulse width modulation: telling a servo where to point by how long each pulse lasts. Typically 1.0 ms is one end, 1.5 ms the middle and 2.0 ms the other end.
Checking the result and correcting it. A servo measures its angle and keeps pushing until it's right.
Control that uses feedback: it acts, checks, and corrects.
A motor that turns in tiny, exact steps, usually 200 to go all the way around (1.8° per step).
Control without feedback: it does the steps but never checks where it ended up.
When the load is too heavy or the steps come too fast, a stepper misses some, and nothing tells it.
How strongly a stopped stepper holds its position.
Moving each motor until a part taps a switch at the edge, so the machine knows exactly where it is. 3D printers do it before every print.
A DC motor with a gearbox. Good at spinning nonstop, like a robot car's wheels.
A very fast, powerful and efficient motor with no brushes rubbing inside. It needs a speed controller (ESC).
Electronic speed controller: a small computer that switches a brushless motor's coils.
A stiff part of a robot arm, like the bones in your arm.
Where links connect and move, like your shoulder and elbow. Turning joints rotate like a hinge; sliding joints move in a straight line.
Each joint that can move on its own adds one. Two let an arm reach spots on a flat surface; six let it reach and point anywhere.
Working out where the hand ends up from the joint angles you picked.
Working backwards: finding the joint angles that put the hand on a spot. The robot's computer solves it with trigonometry.
The unit hobby servos use for their strength (torque). A 2 kg·cm servo can hold 2 kg at 1 cm, or 200 g at 10 cm.
A weight on the other side of a joint that balances the load, like the one on a crane.
A choice that gives something and costs something, because engineers can't have everything.
How much stuff something is made of, measured in kilograms (kg). In everyday talk, and in Bot Arena, we call this weight.
How hard gravity pulls on something: mass × 9.8, measured in newtons. In everyday talk, and in Bot Arena, we say kilograms.
The pull of the Earth that makes things fall and gives them weight.
The unit for forces like thrust and weight. On Earth, 1 kg weighs about 9.8 newtons (N).
Every push has an equal push back. Thrusters push air down, so the air pushes the car up.
The push from an engine or thruster. Blasting air down out of nozzles pushes the car up.
Thrust ÷ weight. Above 1.0, the thrusters can lift the car by themselves.
In the Flying Car Lab, the total upward push from all your lift nozzles.
How fast something is going when it hits the ground: about √(2 × 9.8 × height). It grows with the square root of the height.
Say what you think will happen, and why, before you test.
Try it and see what really happens. A fair test changes only one thing at a time.
Say why it happened, using what you saw and measured.
Change one thing and test again.
How well tires hold the road. Tires with more grip can take corners faster without sliding, but they roll a little less easily on the straights.
How steep a hill is, measured in degrees. Steeper hills need more torque to climb.
How long the thrusters can fire before the air runs out.

def.cadet: Changed after it was made, like a picture with something stuck in later.
def.recruit: Changed after it was made. An altered Echo has something added, removed or changed, so it tells a different story.
def.operative: Edited after it was made, so it no longer shows what really happened. An altered source fails at least one check.

def.cadet: A clue that shows what really happened.
def.recruit: Something you can check that shows whether a thing is true, like a date, a shadow or a matching copy.
def.operative: Something in a source, or about it, that can be checked and that supports or disproves a claim. A guess isn't evidence.
